perspectives.who: Traders in the Indus Valley and other early cities
perspectives.explanation: They weighed goods by putting them in one pan and standard stone weights in the other. The balance never told them a number. It only told them which side was heavier.
A balance compares how much matter two things hold, which is called mass. Gravity pulls both pans the same, so the balance still works on the Moon. A spring scale would read much less there.
Splitting 6 coins as 5 and 1, or 4 and 2, shows that one amount can be made in many ways. Nothing is added or lost.
The = sign means 'is the same amount as'. It does not mean 'now write the answer'. Many children first read it as 'the answer comes next', and that makes later algebra harder.
A number sentence is a statement, and a statement can be true or false. 2 + 2 = 5 is a perfectly good sentence. It is just false.
In many programming languages one = puts a value into a box, and two together (==) ask 'are these the same?'. The same sign can be an order or a question, depending on the language.
You can add coins to the light pan, or take coins from the heavy pan, until both sides match.

The Baghdad mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on al-jabr, 'restoring', and al-muqabala, 'balancing'. His idea was to fix an uneven equation by putting back what is missing, or removing what is extra, on both sides.

Al-Khwarizmi (about 820 CE) and the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta (628 CE) both solved equations by keeping both sides equal while changing them. Doing the same to both sides is the heart of their methods.

The balance picture works well for whole numbers. It gets awkward with negative numbers, because a pan cannot hold less than nothing. So algebra keeps the rule 'do the same to both sides' and lets go of the pans.
In 2001 they reported that bees learned a rule, 'choose the same as before', and used it with colours and patterns they had never seen. They took this as a sign that bees can grasp 'same' as an idea.
Some scientists ask whether simpler kinds of learning could explain the result. They want more tests before saying how bees think. Both groups agree that bees do far more than react by habit.
In the 1700s Linnaeus sorted plants and animals into groups by features he could see. His method is still the base of how living things are named.
Scientists who study how traditional peoples name nature find that many sort plants by use, place or smell: what heals, what feeds, what grows by water. Each sorting rule is right for its purpose.
A count of each group is called a frequency. It shows how a whole set is spread out. 'Most' always depends on the rule that made the groups.
Many animals, such as fish and bees, pick the bigger group of food or friends without using number words. So noticing 'more' is older than counting with numbers.
Sorts by use: leaves for the pot, flowers for the altar, roots for the medicine. The same plants are put together in different ways for different jobs.
Sorts living beings today by who their ancestors were, using DNA as well as what can be seen. Whales end up beside cows, not beside fish.
Piaget's famous tests found that young children often think the number changes when things are spread out. They have not yet fixed the idea that moving does not change how many.
The number in a set is a fact about the set itself, not about how it is arranged. Spread out or heaped up, six things are still six.
Notches cut on bones, such as the Ishango bone from Africa, may be some of the oldest tallies. One cut stands for one thing, which people have used for tens of thousands of years.
Many Chinese people tally in fives with the strokes of the character 正, while many Europeans cross four lines with a fifth. Different groups, same idea of one mark each.

Biologists meet this all the time. Euglena is a tiny living being that has green chloroplasts like a plant and swims like an animal. Scientists had to decide where to put it, and the choice has changed over time.
He pointed out that the things we call games do not share one feature. They are linked by overlapping likenesses, like a family. Some things belong to a group without fitting a clean rule.
The Greek thinker Aristotle sorted animals by how they live and breed. He believed sorting is how we find the order of nature.
Some biologists remind us that nature is a smooth spread, and the lines between groups are ones we draw. Sorting is a tool for thinking, not a list that nature handed us.
Lay two sticks from the same line. The one that reaches further is longer. At walking speeds this is always true.
Length depends a little on how fast the thing moves compared with the observer. At near light speed a moving stick measures shorter. We never notice this on Earth.
Lothal and Mohenjo-daro had scales with fine marked lines cut into ivory and shell. Their bricks were made to one set of lengths, so walls could line up.
They used a royal cubit rod, a set length measured from the elbow to the fingertip. The same rod was carried from site to site so everyone shared one start line.
Piaget found that children under about six often think a stick that is pushed forward has become longer. Understanding that moving does not change length is a step in thinking.
On a hot day a metal bar grows a tiny bit longer, and a very fast bar measures a tiny bit shorter. Moving does not change length for everyday sticks. Heat and extreme speed can.
They straighten the rope or tape to read a length. The straight length is the one you can compare.

perspectives.who: Lewis Fry Richardson and Benoit Mandelbrot
perspectives.explanation: They noticed that a coastline measured with a short ruler comes out longer than with a long one, because small bends keep appearing. For crinkly things, how long depends on the size of your ruler.
Use separate words: a tall tree, a long rope, a high shelf. Tall and high go up, and long goes any way.
Often use one word, lamba, for both a long road and a tall person. The same measure is named differently, so our words do not cut the world in exactly the same places.
Young children often compare only neighbours and get stuck. Putting a whole row in order, called seriation, is a skill that grows with age.
If A is shorter than B and B is shorter than C, then A is shorter than C. This rule, called transitivity, lets us put any number of things in order without comparing every pair.
Surveyors called harpedonaptai used knotted ropes to mark lines and right angles for building. A rope carried a length from place to place.

perspectives.who: Builders in the Vedic Indian tradition
perspectives.explanation: The Shulba Sutras, old manuals for building altars, explain how to use cords (rajju) to make squares and circles of exact size. The cord was the measuring tool.
Used place value and a symbol for zero, with ten as the base. Aryabhata, in 499 CE, wrote numbers in this way, and the idea travelled to the Arab world and Europe.
Used place value with a base of sixty, which is why we still have sixty minutes in an hour. The Maya of Central America used twenty. Ten is one choice among many.
Say 'eleven' and 'twelve', words that do not show 'ten and one'. Hindi 11 to 19 are also separate words. Children must learn each.
Say 'ten-one', 'ten-two', and so on. Studies find that children who count in this way often grasp tens and ones sooner.
Count in tens because we have ten fingers. Many number systems around the world are built on ten.
Are reported to have counted in eights, by using the gaps between the fingers rather than the fingers themselves. What you choose to count changes the system.
In Roman numbers, X means ten wherever it stands. The place of a symbol hardly matters, so adding large numbers was hard work.
The same digit means different amounts in different places. This is why 12 and 21 differ, and why a short list of digits can write any number.
On a Chinese suanpan or a bead frame, ten beads in one column are swapped for one bead in the next column. The carrying is done by hand.
Its wheels roll from 9 back to 0 and push the next wheel on by one. A computer counts in twos in the same way, rolling over at 1.
Sanskrit has its own name for each power of ten: eka, dasha, shata, sahasra. An old text, the Yajurveda, lists names up to a million million.
Reached their big unit when sixty sixties made 3600. A hundred was not special for them.
Believed in one fixed space, like an invisible box, where every thing has its own exact place.
Argued that there is no empty box. 'Where' only means 'how far, and which way, from other things'. Most physicists since then have agreed with Leibniz.
A person in Australia and one in India stand on opposite sides of Earth. 'Down' is toward the centre of the planet for both.
In orbit they float and have no up or down. Without gravity, the words 'top' and 'bottom' only mean something if you choose a way to face.
A closed curve has an inside and an outside, and any path from one to the other must cross the line. This is proved as the Jordan curve theorem.
Every living cell has a thin skin called a membrane that decides what is inside and what is outside. It has gates, so 'inside' is kept by careful trading, not by a wall.
Judge near and far by steps or by how big something looks, and the answer changes with the one who judges.
Measures distance by how much of the scenery slides past its eyes as it flies. The scientist Mandyam Srinivasan showed this. For a bee, far means a lot of scenery passed.
Use left and right, which are tied to your own body and turn when you turn.
People in northern Australia use north, south, east and west instead. They would say 'the cup is by your south foot'. The researcher Stephen Levinson found they always know which way they face.
Use the body of a person: in front is the way someone faces.
A Mayan language in Mexico. Its speakers often use uphill and downhill, based on the slope of the land, rather than front and behind.
Call 'left of me' a self-based frame and 'north of the well' a fixed frame. Humans can use both and move between them.
Showed that you cannot tell if a ship is moving from inside it. What counts as 'moving' depends on what you measure against, which is what a frame of reference means.
In his Elements, about 300 BCE, a solid is that which has length, breadth and depth. Greek thinkers such as Plato studied the five regular solids.
Mathematicians who study shapes by stretching and bending say a mug and a doughnut are the same solid shape, since each has one hole. For them the exact shape matters less than how it connects.
A flat face is a perfect plane and a curved surface is a perfect curve. These are ideas that real things only come near.
Look closer, and no table is perfectly flat. Its surface is made of tiny hills and valleys of atoms. 'Flat' depends on how closely we look.
A ball rolls, a box slides. It depends on which part touches the ground.
Rolling also needs friction between the ground and the object. On smooth ice a ball may slide without turning. A cube can tumble over its edges, as a die does.

One tin, two ways.one_view: I asked about scale, scientists, traditions, other beings and history and found no second view. The idea that a tin can roll on its curved side or slide on its flat end is a plain test anyone can repeat with the same result.

perspectives.explanation: Plato described five perfect solids, built from flat faces that are all the same: cube, tetrahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron.
Salt crystals grow as cubes, quartz as six-sided prisms, and many are other solids. Nature builds shapes that do not fit the four families.
Made bricks all in one ratio, 1 to 2 to 4, so they stacked and bonded neatly in tall walls.
Build honeycomb from six-sided tubes that fit together with no gaps. Flat faces let them stack wax cells with the least wax.

Why a cone rolls in a curve.one_view: I asked about scale, scientists, traditions, other beings and history and found no second view. A cone is wider at one end, so one side travels further than the other and it turns in a circle. This is a geometry fact that anyone can test.

perspectives.explanation: The word cylinder comes from kylindros, a Greek word linked to rolling. Sphere comes from sphaira, a ball. The names speak of what the shape does.
Call the same shape yuanzhu, which means round pillar. It names what the shape looks like, not how it moves.
Believed the heavens must be made of perfect spheres, because the sphere was the most perfect shape.
Say gravity pulls big things into a ball, because every part is drawn toward the centre. Small space rocks stay lumpy, like potatoes, because their gravity is too weak to round them.
Have used balance scales, the tula of India, for thousands of years. Heavier goes down.
A balance compares mass, which is how much matter there is. Weight is the pull of gravity. On the Moon a balance still reads the same, while a spring scale reads less.
Used a stone or metal piece kept as the standard. 'As heavy as' meant as heavy as the royal weight.
Redefined the kilogram using a number from physics, called the Planck constant, instead of a metal cylinder kept in Paris. 'The same weight' is now written in the laws of nature.
The old story says that he worked out whether a crown was pure gold by comparing how much water it pushed aside with how heavy it was. He understood that stuff differs in how tightly it is packed.
Call this packing density, the mass in each bit of space. Cotton and iron take the same room and are far apart in density.
Sell grain by weight rather than by counting. Ten heavy things and ten light things are unequal for them even though the number is the same.
Treat counting and measuring differently: counting goes in whole steps, while weight can have any value. A count tells how many, and a weight tells how much.
In the 1780s he weighed everything before and after reactions and showed that the total mass did not change. Matter is moved around but never lost.
Taught that things are built of tiny unchanging atoms (anu) that join and part. A new shape is only a new arrangement.
Call this the size-weight illusion. It was written about by Charpentier in 1891. Even when you know the two weigh the same, your hand still says the small one is heavier.
Use springs or balances. These do not feel expectations. They give the same reading for a small thing and a big thing of the same weight.
Report that animals judge how heavy things are by lifting and testing, and choose what suits the task. They take this as sign of planning.
Say we should check whether the animal is using a simpler cue, like how hard the lift felt. Both agree that the animal pays careful attention to weight.
Calls air vayu and counts it among the five great elements (pancha mahabhuta). It is the element that moves and touches the skin.
Say air is a crowd of tiny gas particles, always moving and bumping into us. We feel wind when they push in one direction, but even still air presses on us all the time.
For centuries traders used the monsoon winds, which blow one way in summer and the other in winter, to sail dhows between India, Arabia and Africa.
Explain that moving air pushes because its particles hit a surface and bounce back, giving it a shove. More speed means more shove.
Speak of prana, the breath, as the life in a being. Without it a body does not live.
Explain that cells use oxygen from air to release energy from food. Yet some microbes, deep in mud, live without oxygen at all, so not every being needs air.
Greek engineer from the first century CE, who showed with upside-down cups in water that air fills a space and keeps water out.
Say air is mostly empty space between gas particles that fly about. It takes up space because the particles keep pushing, not because it is solid stuff.
Called air springy in 1662 and measured how squeezing it into half the space doubled its push. He thought of air as being like tiny coiled springs.
Explained the same result with moving particles. In less space they hit the walls more often, so the push grows.
Knows that a pot with no drainage lets roots rot, because roots in waterlogged soil cannot get air. To most of us, roots do not look like they breathe.
Show that root cells burn food with oxygen like any other cell. Mangrove trees grow special roots that stick up out of the mud, called pneumatophores, to take in air.
Teaches three pillars of life: food (ahara), sleep (nidra) and moderation (brahmacharya). Sleep counts as a need as strong as food.
Tardigrades, tiny animals, can dry out and live for years with almost no water, until rain comes. So the need for water can be paused, though not forever.
The Inuit made fur parkas for deep cold, while people of hot India wore thin cotton. What 'enough' covering means depends on the climate.
Birds weave nests, hermit crabs borrow shells, and bees build wax homes. Many animals make or find shelter.
Stand behind a wall and the wind feels gentle. It seems that the wall stops the air.

Wind tunnel tests show that air swirls into eddies behind a building. Some spots are calm and others have gusts. A windbreak made of trees works better than a solid wall because it slows the air without making swirls.
Teaches that every being with life (jiva) wants to live, from humans to plants, which have one sense. This is the reason for ahimsa, doing no harm.
Find that all life needs energy, water and a way to take in materials. Some microbes near deep-sea vents need no sunlight and no oxygen. So needs are shared, yet differ in detail.

perspectives.who: Sushruta, the surgeon of ancient India
perspectives.explanation: His book, the Sushruta Samhita, described bones in detail for surgery and counted 300, including teeth and soft bones.
Note that many animals have no inside bones. An insect wears its skeleton outside, as an exoskeleton, and a jellyfish has none at all, only water pressure.
Bones are a frame. They hold the body up and protect the heart and brain.
Bone is also a factory and a store. Its soft middle, the marrow, makes blood cells, and it stores calcium that the rest of the body draws on.
Described eight kinds of joints, such as ones that turn, ones that slide and ones shaped like a mortar and pestle. He studied them to set broken and dislocated limbs.
Group joints by how they move, and also by what holds them: ligaments, cartilage and fluid. A joint is a whole working part, not only the place where two bones meet.
See the elbow as a hinge and the hip as a ball and socket, and use these ideas to design robots and artificial hips.
Point out that an octopus arm has no bones and no joints, and still it can bend anywhere along its length. Joints are one solution, not the only one.
The Greek doctor Galen, about 170 CE, taught that nerves carry a spirit that makes muscles pull.
In 1954 two scientists, unrelated, showed that muscle works by thin threads of protein sliding past one another, which makes the muscle shorter. This is called the sliding filament theory.
A skeleton in a museum looks dry and dead, like a stick. Many people think bones are just hard props.
A living bone is full of blood and busy cells. Some cells build bone and others take it apart. The whole skeleton is slowly replaced, which is how a broken bone mends.
Count 206 bones in a grown-up and about 270 or more in a newborn. Several bones fuse as a child grows.
The count depends on the rule. Sushruta's 300 included cartilages and teeth. Some people have an extra rib or tiny extra bones, so 206 is a usual number, not a law.
Vinegar and baking soda make carbon dioxide, water and sodium acetate. It is easy to remember and right.

The acid first reacts with the baking soda to make carbonic acid, which then breaks into water and carbon dioxide. Joseph Black, in the 1750s, was the first to study this gas, which he called fixed air.
Bubbles, colour change, heat, light and a solid forming tell us a reaction has happened.
Warn that each sign can happen without a new substance. Boiling makes bubbles, and dissolving can change colour. To be sure, chemists measure, such as testing what the substance now is.
Rusting is iron reacting with oxygen and water to form iron oxide. It works like a tiny battery with a wet surface, which is why salty air rusts iron faster.

This pillar, about 1,600 years old, has hardly rusted. Studies find the iron has phosphorus in it, which helps a thin protective layer form on the surface. The old smiths made a metal that resists rust.
Sodium is a soft metal that burns water and chlorine is a poison gas. Together they make table salt, which we eat. The product is nothing like its parents.
The old alchemists of Arabia, India (rasashastra) and Europe searched for ways to change one metal into another. Their work led to many tools and methods of chemistry, though not to gold.
Before 1800 many scientists, including Lavoisier, pictured heat as a fluid called caloric that flowed into and out of things.
In the 1840s he showed that heat is a form of energy. He stirred water with a paddle and measured the warmth. Reactions give out or take in energy, which often shows up as heat.
Taught that the heavens were made of an unchanging fifth substance, so changes of matter belonged to Earth alone.
Find with telescopes that space has chemistry. Molecules such as water and alcohol form on cold dust grains between stars. The amino acid glycine was found in comet dust.

perspectives.who: Cooks who use the absorption method
perspectives.explanation: Measure water so the grain soaks up everything, and nothing is thrown away.
Many families boil rice in a lot of water and pour off the starchy water, the kanji. Food scientists explain that the starch swells and sets free part of itself, so draining changes the texture.
Turns curd to butter, and butter to ghee, a food prized for cooking and medicine. Slow heat gives ghee its fragrance.
Explain that butter is fat with a little water and milk solids mixed in. Heating boils away the water and browns the solids, which are strained out. They cannot be mixed back, so ghee stays ghee.
Black ink looks like one colour, and it seems to be a simple thing.
In the early 1900s this Russian botanist split green leaf colour into bands by passing it through a column of chalk. He named the method chromatography, 'colour writing'. Black ink is also a mixture.
A dye clings to the paper's surface, and the water carries it along, pulling it away. A strong clinger moves little.
Their 1941 work, awarded a Nobel Prize in 1952, treated the water as one layer and the paper's wet fibres as another. A dye divides itself between them, and how it divides decides how far it goes.
Permanent ink is permanent. It will never come off or move.
A substance only moves if the liquid can dissolve it. Permanent ink does not dissolve in water but does dissolve in alcohol. Forensic chemists choose liquids to match the ink.
For about thirty years his method was ignored, until other scientists picked it up in the 1930s.
Use chromatography to test blood for medicines, food for poisons and air for pollution. It is one of the most used tools of chemistry.
In 1860 they showed that each element glows with its own colour pattern in a flame, and used it to discover two new elements, caesium and rubidium.
Explained the colours from 1913: each atom has levels of energy for its electrons. When an electron drops down a level, it gives out light of one exact colour.
In the 1600s he found that syrup of violets turned red with acid and green with base. This was an early indicator.
Have long used turmeric, which turns red with soap or lime. The kumkum used in worship is made from turmeric and slaked lime, a chemical test used as a tradition.
A Danish chemist who invented the pH scale in 1909 at the Carlsberg brewery, to keep track of acids in beer making.
Found that the scale has limits and other ways to say acid. Some definitions, like those of Arrhenius, Bronsted and Lowry, and Lewis, cover different cases.
In the 1880s he explained neutralising as acid's hydrogen ions joining with base's hydroxide ions to make water.
In 1923 each independently said an acid hands a hydrogen ion to a base. This also works in liquids that are not water.
Make formic acid to hurt or warn off a predator. The word formic comes from formica, the Latin for ant.
Bacteria that turn milk to curd make lactic acid. The sour acid keeps harmful microbes out, so the curd keeps.
Many thought rubber and similar stuff were clumps of small molecules held by loose forces. They doubted that molecules could be so long.
In the 1920s he argued that they are truly giant molecules with strong bonds along the whole chain. He was doubted at first and won the Nobel Prize in 1953.
Say the borate links are weak and come apart again. That is why slime flows slowly yet stretches and snaps.
In 1839 he found that heating rubber with sulphur makes strong, lasting links between chains. His rubber does not flow, unlike slime.
In India, people have for centuries used the silk of silkworms and the lac made by lac insects, for cloth and bangles. Living beings made these polymers long before chemistry named them.
Find that proteins, cellulose, starch and DNA are all polymers. Life is built from chains, and the order of links carries the information.
Made Bakelite in 1907, the first fully man-made plastic. It was hailed as the material of a thousand uses.
Today find plastic waste in oceans and even tiny bits of plastic inside living beings. The same long chains that make plastic strong make it slow to break down.
In 1916 and 1918 they proposed collision theory: particles must bump into each other to react, and only hard enough bumps count.
In 1935 he added that particles in a bump form a brief, unstable joined state before turning into the new substances. This transition-state theory explains details that simple collisions cannot.

Reaction rate: how fast a change goes.one_view: I asked about scale, scientists, traditions, other beings and history and found no second view. Rate is a measuring rule, an amount of change divided by time, and every chemist uses it in exactly the same way.

perspectives.explanation: In 1864 they showed that a reaction goes at a rate that depends on how much of each substance is left, so as the reactants run out, it slows.
In the 1950s this Soviet chemist found a mixture whose colour kept swinging between yellow and clear, so its rate rose and fell. His work was doubted for years. Not every reaction just slows down.
In 1889 he showed that a small rise in temperature greatly raises a reaction's rate, because more particles have enough energy to react.
Note that this fails for living things when heat goes too far. An enzyme, the helper protein in a cell, loses its shape in high heat and stops working. Past a point warmth slows a living reaction.
Explain that stirring brings fresh particles to meet, as above.
Find that in big factory tanks, how fast things mix is often the limit, more than the chemistry. They design the stirring and pumps as carefully as the recipe.
Explain that a powder has more surface touching the other substance, so more particles can react at once.
Know that fine dust, such as flour or coal dust, can catch fire and explode, because every tiny grain burns at once. Many accidents have taught this.
Say more particles in the same space meet more often, so the reaction is faster.
Point out that the inside of a cell is very crowded with proteins. This crowding changes how fast reactions inside cells go, and so a test tube is a poor copy of a cell.
In 1835 he used the word catalysis for a hidden power that helps reactions along without being used up. He did not know how it worked.
Defined a catalyst in 1894 as something that speeds a reaction without being used up, and received the Nobel Prize in 1909. Today we say it gives the reaction an easier path.
Used salt, oil and spices to keep fruits and vegetables for months. They slowed rot long before anyone knew about microbes.
Add substances called inhibitors, such as antioxidants, that block the particles that cause spoiling. It is the same goal reached with different tools.
Notice no change in a stone or a glass window, and think nothing is happening.
Find that rocks are slowly changing all the time, as rain and air dissolve and rust them over thousands of years. Slow is not the same as still.
In the 1700s he sorted plants by counting their stamens and other parts, which anyone could check. His system was easy to use, though it grouped some unrelated plants.
Sort by ancestry too, using DNA, so that groups match family trees. The rule is no longer only what we can see.
Saw that differences among members of one kind are what natural selection works on. Variety is the raw material of change.
Described an older habit of mind, typological thinking, where each kind has a perfect pattern and differences are errors. He argued for population thinking, where the variety is the real thing.
For long, many people thought that rot and maggots arose from dead things by themselves.
In the 1860s he showed with careful flasks that rot starts only when living microbes reach the food. Rot is the work of living beings.
Fungi were treated as plants with no green, because they grow in one place and have cell walls.
In 1969 he placed fungi in their own kingdom. Later DNA studies showed fungi are closer cousins to animals than to plants. Both fungi and animals eat food made by others.
Decomposers need warmth, water, food and air. Without them, rot stops.

Peat bogs have almost no oxygen and are acid, so rot is very slow. The Tollund Man, about 2,300 years old, was found in a Danish bog with his skin still preserved. Some microbes rot food without air, so air is not always needed.
Dried grains, salted fish, pickled mangoes and made ghee. Each way takes away water or changes the food so microbes cannot grow.
A French confectioner who, around 1809, found that food heated in sealed jars stayed fresh. It was one of the first steps to canning, many years before microbes were known.
Called earthworms the intestines of the earth, a view that they work the soil.
Spent decades on worms. His last book, in 1881, measured that worms bring up and turn over tons of soil per acre every year. Many farmers had thought worms were pests.
An old Indian text says that beings are born from food and return to the earth to become food. It sees life as one turning circle.

Trace the same cycle in atoms of carbon, nitrogen and others that pass from soil to plants to animals and back through decomposers. They also find that some leave the cycle for long times, as coal or limestone.
In the 1700s he guessed that electricity moves from the positive end to the negative end. That direction is still used in diagrams, called conventional current.
Found in 1897 that what moves in a wire is the electron, which has negative charge, so it goes the other way. Both ways of drawing the flow work for circuits.
For a simple torch circuit, the bulb lights whether the wire is straight, curly or knotted.
Showed in the 1830s that a coil of wire carrying current behaves differently from a straight one. It makes a magnet. For fast changing current, shape matters a great deal.
In 1879 each made a lamp by heating a thin thread, the filament, in a glass bulb until it glowed white hot.
Say an LED makes light in another way: electrons drop to a lower energy level inside a crystal and give out light, with little heat. It is also an example of a switch from hot light to cool light.
The big number of volts makes the wall dangerous.
Say that it is the current, the amount of electricity through the body, that does the harm, and the path it takes. A small current through the heart can be deadly, and wet skin lets more through.
A bird on a single wire has both feet at the same voltage, so no electricity needs to flow through its body.
Find that big birds such as eagles are killed when their wings touch two wires or a wire and a pole. The difference in voltage across the body is what counts.
In the 1780s Galvani saw a frog's leg twitch from electricity and thought animals made their own electricity. Volta argued that two metals produced it. Both were partly right.
Use a shock on purpose. A defibrillator sends a strong electric pulse to stop a heart beating wildly, so that it can start again in step.
Add layers: insulated wires, earth wires, fuses and switches that cut off power in a fraction of a second.
Note that harm depends on how big the current is, how long it flows and where it goes. A small current for a short time may be felt only; a small current through the chest can be deadly.
Imagine electricity as water pushed around a pipe loop by a pump. It helps us see why a loop is needed.
Show with the work of John Poynting in 1884 that the energy of a circuit travels in the space around the wires, as electric and magnetic fields. The wires guide the energy.
When the loop is cut, the whole circuit goes dead at once.
Say the change spreads along the wire at close to the speed of light, so it seems at once. The electrons themselves drift at only a fraction of a millimetre per second.
In 1729 he discovered that electricity could pass along some materials, like wet thread, and not others, like silk. He gave us the first idea of conductors and insulators.
Find a middle group, semiconductors, such as silicon. They sometimes conduct and sometimes do not, and computers are made of them. Even air conducts in lightning.
A switch is a gap that is closed or opened with a lever, by hand.
In 1947 they invented the transistor, a switch with no moving part that is turned on and off by a tiny electric signal. A modern phone holds billions of them.
In 1822 he wrote the mathematical law of how heat flows through a solid, without saying anything about atoms.
Explained later that atoms in the hot part jiggle faster and bump their neighbours, passing on energy bump by bump.
Explain the slow spread by Fourier's heat equation: heat spreads in all directions, not in a straight race, so far points warm much later.
Know it from experience, and choose wood or plastic handles for pans so that the heat does not reach the hand.
Group materials by how fast they pass heat: metals fast, wood and plastic slowly, still air very slowly.
Use insulation to live. Fur and feathers trap still air, and penguins and whales have a thick layer of fat. They make their own insulators.
In 1900 he pictured a metal as a sea of free electrons that carry heat and electricity quickly.
Found that this picture is only part of the story. Diamond has no free electrons yet conducts heat better than metals, because its tightly bound atoms pass on vibrations quickly.
In 1800 he found invisible heat rays beyond the red end of sunlight, now called infrared.
These snakes have small pits on their face that sense infrared. They feel the heat of a warm mouse in the dark, a sense we do not have.
Made a thermoscope around 1600, a glass tube with air and water that rose and fell with warmth, but with no numbers.
In 1742 he made a scale from the freezing and boiling of water. His scale at first ran the other way, with 0 for boiling.
Use liquid thermometers, each made for a range.
Read a forehead or a pan by the infrared heat it gives off, with no touching. They measure radiation, not expansion.
In 1850 he stated that heat never moves by itself from a cooler to a warmer body. It is a basic law of nature.
Argued that it is an overwhelming chance, not a certainty. With countless particles, it is so unlikely that heat flows from cold to warm that it never happens in practice.
In the 1760s he was the first to clearly separate the two ideas, and measured how much heat different substances hold.
In 1798 he watched cannon barrels being drilled and saw that rubbing seemingly made endless heat. He argued that heat is a kind of motion, and not a fluid.
Described in 1690 a test of three bowls of water, hot, cold and warm. A hand from the hot bowl feels the warm bowl cold, while a hand from the cold bowl feels it hot.
Find that our skin has sensors that react to change in temperature, not temperature itself. A thermometer's number does not depend on a hand's past.
In the 1860s he bred pea plants and found that features pass on as separate units. The units later got the name genes.
Thought for a time that features blend like paint. If so, differences would soon fade away, and he worried over this.
Showed that a seed carries inherited units from both parent plants. Features such as flower colour pass on by clear rules.
Find that the way a plant lives, such as drought or cold, can switch genes on or off, and some of these switches may pass to its seeds. The seed carries more than the written code.
Taught that a thing keeps moving only while something pushes it. When the push stops, the motion stops.
Showed that a moving thing keeps going the same way and speed unless a force acts on it. A push along its way speeds it up and a push against slows it.
A French scholar of the 1300s who thought a push puts a kind of force in a thing, called impetus, and a bigger push puts more in.
In 1687 stated that the change in motion is bigger when the force is bigger. Force equals mass times change in speed, and impetus is not needed.
Little clay toy carts with wheels have been found at Harappan sites. The wheel was used in play and work.
Say rolling takes much less effort than sliding, because the part touching the ground is momentarily still. Friction is far smaller for rolling.

A rolling thing's shape steers it.one_view: I asked about scale, scientists, traditions, other beings and history and found no second view. A thing that is wider at one end travels further on that side, so it turns in a curve, and anyone can test this with a cup.

perspectives.explanation: Explain that a ball stores energy in its squashed shape and gives it back. Each bounce is lower because some energy turns to heat and sound.
Find that a flea jumps by squashing a pad of springy protein called resilin and letting it go. Living bodies also bounce.
Say a spinning top has angular momentum, which resists tipping. When it slows, the pull of gravity wins.

Show that the Earth is itself a spinning top. Its axis wobbles in a slow circle, once in about 26,000 years, like a top that is leaning. Indian children have long played with the spinning top, called bambaram or lattu.
In 1660 he found that a spring pushes back in proportion to how far it is stretched. This is Hooke's law.
Find that living beings store energy in springy parts too. In a human leg the Achilles tendon stretches like a spring and gives back energy on each step.
Taught that things naturally rest, and that all motion needs a pusher.

In 1687 stated his first law: a still thing stays still and a moving thing keeps moving the same way, unless a force acts. In the Vaisheshika school of India, motion was a basic idea caused by effort or impact.
A push is away from you and a pull is toward you, as you feel it in the hand.
Newton showed that forces come in pairs, and when you push a wall the wall pushes back. Einstein later pictured gravity not as a pull but as the bending of space and time.
Thought an arrow keeps flying because the air pushes it from behind. A big push sends it far.
Showed that the arrow keeps moving because nothing strong stops it. A bigger push gives more speed, and air and the ground slowly stop it.
Said that a heavy thing has more mass, which is a measure of how much it resists being moved. The harder to start, the bigger the mass.
In 1915 pointed out that this resistance to being moved and the heaviness we feel from gravity are exactly equal for every thing, and treated this as a clue to how gravity works.
The Greek thinker of the 200s BCE is said to have worked out how to move a ship with a compound of pulleys and a rope.
Followers of Mozi wrote about 2,300 years ago on levers and pulleys. They were practical, and studied how machines save effort.
Is credited with showing that more rope turns can lift a big load with a small pull.
Explain it by energy: with two ropes, the pull is half but you pull twice as far. The work you do stays the same.
Argued in the 1600s that what is kept in motion is the product of mass and speed.

Argued that what counts is mass times speed squared, which he called vis viva. This quarrel, which went on for decades, ended when scientists saw that both quantities are useful but different. The term work came in 1829.
A 12th century Indian mathematician who described a wheel with weights on its rim that he believed would turn forever. It was an early perpetual motion idea.
Showed in the 1840s that work lost to friction turns into heat, so nothing is truly lost, and no machine can turn forever without a fresh supply of energy.
An ancient Greek device made around the 100s BCE. It had dozens of bronze gears to follow the Sun, Moon and eclipses.
In 2013 scientists found that the young planthopper Issus has gear teeth on its hind legs, which keep its legs in step as it jumps.
Tradition says he designed a water screw, a tube wound round a rod, to lift water. It is still used in places.
See the same shape in snail shells and in climbing vines. The ramp wound round is a shape that lets a small turning do a big job.
Split huge stone blocks by hammering wooden wedges in rows and soaking them with water, so they swelled and cracked the rock.
Point out that our own teeth are wedges. Incisors cut and bite by turning a push into a sideways split.
Say that multiplying the gains of simple machines can give a very big advantage, though each part loses a little to friction.
See the human body as many levers working together. The bones, muscles and joints of the arm and the leg make a compound machine that was never designed.
Until the 1800s many held that living things ran on a special life force that was not made of ordinary matter.
Found that cells have real machines. Paul Boyer and John Walker earned the Nobel Prize in 1997 for explaining ATP synthase, a tiny rotor that turns to make the cell's fuel.
Make kumkum for worship by mixing turmeric and slaked lime, which turns the yellow powder red. Cooks have long seen turmeric stain turn red with soap.
Explain that the yellow colouring in turmeric, curcumin, changes colour in alkali. This is why turmeric is an indicator, and why lemon juice, an acid, turns it back.
Have taught red, yellow and blue as the three main paints. Mixing them goes toward brown and gets darker.
Use cyan, magenta and yellow for ink, and red, green and blue for light. Mixing lights gets brighter, since each adds light, but mixing paint takes light away.
Ancient Greek thinkers taught that our eyes send out rays that touch things and make them seen. Plato also thought this.
In about 1011 to 1021 in Cairo he showed that light enters the eye from things, after bouncing off them. He wrote it in his Book of Optics and tested it with experiments.
Say light is made when energy changes form. A hot filament, a flame or an LED turns another kind of energy into light each moment, and the light itself is never stored.
Make cold light by a chemical reaction in their bodies, using luciferin. They glow with almost no heat, which the light bulb cannot do.
